Heat capacity for a two-dimensional linear fermion dispersion (C+​=9gζ(3)AkB3​T2/(4πℏ2v2))

Words: 59
Quantum ideal-gas statistics OurBigBook.com
For g copies of a positive-energy branch E=ℏv∣k∣ in area A, the density of states is D(E)=gAE/(2πℏ2v2). At zero chemical potential, the thermal energy is 3gζ(3)A(kB​T)3/(4πℏ2v2), giving the displayed fixed-zero-chemical-potential heat capacity. If a symmetric filled negative-energy band also supplies holes, its excitation energy contributes an equal amount. Counting cones, spin species and holes explicitly is necessary before assigning an absolute numerical coefficient.

Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics (f(E)≃e(μ−E)/(kB​T))

Words: 54 Articles: 1
Quantum ideal-gas statistics OurBigBook.com
Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics describes a dilute classical gas whose single-particle occupation factors have the displayed exponential form. It is the low-occupation classical limit of Bose--Einstein and Fermi--Dirac statistics. Integrating this factor over momentum gives the nonrelativistic Maxwell--Boltzmann number density when the particle energy is mc2+p2/(2m).

n=gs​(h22πmkB​T​)3/2e(μ−mc2)/(kB​T).

Fermi level (μ)

Words: 30
Quantum ideal-gas statistics OurBigBook.com
The Fermi level is the chemical potential controlling electron occupations. For an ideal Fermi gas at zero temperature it equals the Fermi energy; at nonzero temperature the chemical potential need not equal that zero-temperature energy.

Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution (s=kB​T/m​)

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Quantum ideal-gas statistics OurBigBook.com
The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution describes the random velocities and speeds of particles in a classical ideal gas at thermal equilibrium. Individual particles keep changing velocity through collisions, while the equilibrium probability distribution stays fixed. For one species of particle mass m at positive temperature T, the characteristic scale is
s=mkB​T​​,
(3)
where kB​ is the Boltzmann constant. A signed velocity component follows a normal distribution; the nonnegative magnitude follows the Maxwell speed distribution. Their peaks differ because a speed measurement groups together all directions of motion.
Use the gas rest frame, three spatial dimensions, and nonrelativistic particles, with kB​T≪mc2 where c is the speed of light. Assume a dilute gas whose interactions between encounters can be neglected in the ideal gas approximation and whose translational motion is classical. A sufficient condition for negligible quantum exchange effects is nλ3≪1, where n is the number density and λ the thermal de Broglie wavelength. Diluteness alone does not guarantee thermal equilibrium; the gas must have equilibrated. These are the assumptions behind the classical Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution. [ref] [ref]
The connection to Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics is the Boltzmann factor for translational kinetic energy, Ekin​=m∣v∣2/2. Normalizing e−Ekin​/(kB​T) over velocity gives a probability density; an occupation factor e(μ−E)/(kB​T) instead specifies a mean occupation, with chemical potential μ. Their normalizations serve different purposes. [ref]
This connects microscopic motion to measurements: a gas thermometer uses the ideal gas law, collisions and the mean free path govern transport, and measurements of spectral lines use thermal Doppler broadening to infer temperature. Each probes a different aspect of the same thermal motion.
In 1860, James Clerk Maxwell presented the component and speed laws in Part I, Proposition IV of Illustrations of the Dynamical Theory of Gases, pp. 22–23. His argument combined independence of the three velocity components with isotropy, and he explicitly compared the component law with the normal distribution of observational errors. Independence is an assumption of that argument; perpendicular coordinate axes alone do not establish it. [ref]

Wall-impact speed distribution

Words: 50
Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution OurBigBook.com
The speed distribution of atoms striking a wall is weighted by the normal component of velocity, relative to the distribution of atoms present in the bulk. For an isotropic classical monatomic gas, the impact speed density is proportional to v3e−mv2/(2kB​T), and the mean impact kinetic energy is 2kB​T, rather than 3kB​T/2.

Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution (f(v))

Words: 856 Articles: 6
Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution OurBigBook.com
In the gas rest frame, the Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution is the probability density function per unit volume in velocity space:
f(v)=(2πkB​Tm​)3/2exp(−2kB​Tm∣v∣2​)=(2πs2)3/2e−∣v∣2/(2s2)​,∫R3​f(v)d3v=1.
(4)
Thus f(v)d3v gives the probability of a small three-dimensional velocity region. For a gas with bulk mean velocity V, replace v by v−V; the Maxwell speed distribution then describes the magnitude relative to that bulk motion.
For any one Cartesian velocity component vx​, integrating out the other two gives
q(vx​)=2π​s1​e−vx2​/(2s2),⟨vx​⟩=0,⟨vx2​⟩=s2=mkB​T​.
(5)
The factorization f(v)=q(vx​)q(vy​)q(vz​) establishes independence: all three components are centered normal random variables, with variance s2. Both the component density q and the vector density f have their largest values at zero. This concerns densities for small equal-sized regions; any single exact velocity still has probability zero. [ref]
The standard deviation s measures thermal motion even though the mean velocity is zero. Positive and negative components cancel in the mean, but their squares add. This is why thermal Doppler broadening measures a nonzero line width in a gas with no bulk motion.

Maxwell speed distribution (g(v))

Words: 502 Articles: 1
Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution OurBigBook.com
The Maxwell speed distribution is the probability density function for the magnitude v=∣v∣. Unlike a signed velocity component, speed cannot be negative:
g(v)=4πv2(2πkB​Tm​)3/2e−mv2/(2kB​T)=π2​​s3v2​e−v2/(2s2),v≥0.
(6)
For 0≤a<b, the probability of a speed in [a,b] is ∫ab​g(v)dv, and ∫0∞​g(v)dv=1. The density has units of inverse speed, so its height alone is not a probability. [ref]
All velocities with magnitudes from v to v+dv occupy a thin spherical shell of volume 4πv2dv in velocity space. The isotropy of the Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution makes its density constant over each shell, giving g(v)=4πv2f(vex​) for any fixed unit direction ex​. A larger radius offers more directions and more volume. The increasing shell factor initially wins over the decreasing Boltzmann factor, so g(0)=0 and the most probable speed is positive. This is the geometric reason that the peaks of the vector and speed densities disagree.
With the dimensionless quantity u=v/s, every such gas has the same rescaled speed density:
g(v)dv=h(u)du,h(u)=π2​​u2e−u2/2,u≥0.
(7)
For comparison, w=vx​/s has the standard normal distribution density ϕ(w)=e−w2/2/2π​ on the whole real line. The Maxwell speed distribution is neither the positive half of this curve nor the distribution of ∣vx​∣: it combines three components.
The first two moments of the Maxwell speed distribution give the mean and root mean square:
⟨v⟩=π8​​s,⟨v2⟩=3s2,vrms​=⟨v2⟩​=3​s.
(8)
Consequently the mean translational kinetic energy is m⟨v2⟩/2=3kB​T/2, as required by the equipartition theorem. [ref] The mean speed weights fast particles more than the density peak does, and the root mean square weights them more strongly still.
Changing temperature or particle mass only changes s∝T/m​. At fixed mass, four times the temperature doubles every characteristic speed; at fixed temperature, four times the mass halves them. A stretched density becomes lower so that its area stays one. For two species at the same temperature, equal mean translational kinetic energy therefore means different typical speeds.
Most probable speed in the Maxwell distribution (vmp​=2kB​T/m​)
Words: 182
Maxwell speed distribution OurBigBook.com
The most probable speed is the mode, or density maximum, of the Maxwell speed distribution:
vmp​=m2kB​T​​=2​s.
(9)
For small equal-width speed bins, the bin near vmp​ contains the largest expected fraction of particles. This does not mean that any exact speed has positive probability, or that every particle has this speed. The three common summaries obey
svmp​​=2​≈1.414,s⟨v⟩​=π8​​≈1.596,svrms​​=3​≈1.732,
(10)
so vmp​<⟨v⟩<vrms​. The first describes a density peak, the second the mean speed, and the third the root mean square associated with kinetic energy. [ref]
For a concrete scale s=300ms−1, these are approximately 424, 479, and 520ms−1. The most probable velocity vector and each most probable component remain zero in the gas rest frame. A zero vector labels one small region of velocity space, whereas a positive speed labels an entire spherical shell.
A short check uses the derivative of the logarithm of the Maxwell speed distribution for v>0:
dvd​logg(v)=v2​−s2v​.
(11)
It is positive below 2​s and negative above it, locating the unique peak. The factor v2 from the spherical shell supplies the term 2/v; omitting it would incorrectly move the speed peak to zero.

Doppler broadening

Words: 184 Articles: 3
Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution OurBigBook.com
Doppler broadening is the spread of an observed spectral line caused by the distribution of emitter velocities along the line of sight.
Doppler resolution of a Zeeman pattern (Bres​∼3hΔνD​/(2μB​))
Words: 61
Doppler broadening OurBigBook.com
A Maxwellian emitter has Gaussian Doppler frequency FWHM ΔνD​/ν=8kB​Tln2/(mc2)​. Equating this width to the minimum adjacent weak-field sodium component separation 2μB​B/(3h) gives the title resolution scale. A Gaussian blend has no unique resolution threshold: disappearance of individual components and disappearance of the whole broadened multiplet are different criteria. Instrumental resolution, pressure broadening, selected polarization and line strengths must be specified for a sharper prediction.
Thermal Doppler broadening
Words: 101 Articles: 1
Doppler broadening OurBigBook.com
If nonrelativistic emitters of mass m have rest-frame angular frequency ω0​, then the one-dimensional Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution produces a Gaussian line with standard deviation
σω​=cω0​​mkB​T​​.
(12)
Measuring the line width therefore determines the gas temperature when nonthermal broadening is negligible or separately modeled.
Thermal cutoff of Lyman-alpha line widths (bth2​=2kB​T/mH​)
Words: 61
Thermal Doppler broadening OurBigBook.com
A purely thermal hydrogen absorption line has velocity-space optical depth proportional to exp[−(v−v0​)2/b2] with the displayed width. Additional independent Gaussian broadening contributes positive terms to b2. Fitting the lower envelope of width against neutral-hydrogen column density, with numerical calibration for density and pressure smoothing, estimates the temperature-density relation of photoionized intergalactic gas. A single broad line only bounds the temperature from above when its nonthermal width is unknown.

The density of states g(E) is defined so that g(E)dE counts one-particle states with energies in an interval of width dE. A sum over closely spaced states then becomes an integral weighted by g(E).

Anisotropic ideal-gas density of states (N(ε,γ)=γ​N(ε,1))

Words: 64
Density of states OurBigBook.com

The Fermi energy is the highest occupied one-particle energy in the ground state of a noninteracting Fermi gas at zero temperature, measured here relative to the lowest one-particle energy. The Pauli exclusion principle allows only one fermion in each complete one-particle quantum state, including its spin, so adding more particles fills progressively higher energy eigenstates. A cold gas can therefore have substantial kinetic energy even when its temperature is zero. In the thermodynamic limit, with the same energy reference, EF​=μ(T=0) where μ is the chemical potential.[ref]
For a uniform, three-dimensional gas of noninteracting electrons, with spin one-half, equal populations of the two spin states, no applied magnetic field, and nonrelativistic particles of mass m=me​,

Here n is the total number density, V the volume, pF​ the Fermi momentum, ℏ=h/(2π) the reduced Planck constant, and kB​ the Boltzmann constant. The electron Fermi temperature TF​ expresses the same energy scale in kelvin; it is not the actual gas temperature. Strong degeneracy of a degenerate electron gas means T≪TF​. The momentum formula counts states and survives changing the energy–momentum relation, whereas EF​=pF2​/(2m) requires pF​≪mc.[ref]
The reference matters: the displayed EF​ excludes rest energy and sets the zero at p=0. Including rest energy shifts both the one-particle energy and the zero-temperature chemical potential by mc2, leaving occupations unchanged. More generally, adding a constant C to every one-particle energy also adds C to μ; the Fermi-Dirac distribution depends only on their difference. In a finite quantum system the chemical potential at zero temperature can lie between the last occupied and first empty energy eigenstates; its equality with the filling edge is a continuum statement.
At positive temperature, EF​ remains the zero-temperature scale associated with the specified number density. The Fermi level μ(T) must instead satisfy the particle-number condition

(18)
where g(E) is the extensive density of states, including both spin states. Smearing the Fermi-Dirac distribution while arbitrarily holding μ=EF​ generally changes N. This distinction matters when interpreting electron heat capacity and any experiment that infers temperature from an occupation profile.[ref]

Fermi momentum is the magnitude of the momentum at the boundary of filled one-particle states in an isotropic zero-temperature Fermi gas. For the uniform three-dimensional two-component electron model, a short state count gives

To see the factors, impose periodic boundary conditions on a cubic box of side L, so V=L3 and each momentum component is pi​=2πℏji​/L for an integer ji​. Each allowed momentum point occupies a cell of volume (2πℏ/L)3 in momentum space. Divide the sphere volume 4πpF3​/3 by this cell volume and multiply by two for the two spin states. Replacing the discrete count with a volume is the large-box approximation; surface and shell effects are neglected.[ref]
The factor two is not automatic for every Fermi gas. If only one internal state is populated, its number density nσ​ instead satisfies pF,σ​=ℏ(6π2nσ​)1/3. For two equally populated states, nσ​=n/2 recovers the displayed result. Fermi sea
Words: 346 Articles: 1
Fermi energy OurBigBook.com
The Fermi sea is the zero-temperature many-fermion quantum state with every one-particle state below the Fermi energy occupied and every state above it empty. For a uniform isotropic Fermi gas, the occupied region in momentum space is a solid sphere; its boundary is the Fermi surface. These are momenta, not positions: filling the sphere does not put the particles in a ball in ordinary space. Opposite momentum contributions cancel, so the gas at rest has zero total momentum even though its total kinetic energy is positive.
The filled states are forced upward in energy by the Pauli exclusion principle. This is different from the zero-point energy of one particle confined by a boundary. At fixed number density, the Fermi energy remains positive as the box grows to the thermodynamic limit, while the lowest box confinement energy tends to zero. Low-energy excitations move particles from occupied states near the Fermi surface into nearby empty states; deep states have no nearby available destination. This explains why only a small fraction of electrons contribute to the low-temperature electron heat capacity.[ref]

Availability and occupation are different: g(E) is positive above EF​, but at zero temperature those states are empty. The occupied energy distribution is g(E)f(E), with the Fermi-Dirac distribution reduced to f(E)=1 below EF​ and f(E)=0 above it. The convention at the exact boundary does not affect a continuum integral.
With the dimensionless quantity x=E/EF​, the occupied count per dx, divided by the total particle number, is 3x​/2 for 0<x<1. Its area is one. Weighting this by E gives the internal energy and its mean per particle:

At fixed N, EF​∝V−2/3, so the derivative P=−(∂U/∂V)N​ gives the electron degeneracy pressure P=2nEF​/5. The same state-counting geometry therefore predicts a nonzero pressure at zero temperature.
Observation of Fermi pressure in trapped lithium
Words: 229
Fermi energy OurBigBook.com
In 2001, Andrew G. Truscott, Randall G. Hulet, and collaborators observed degeneracy pressure in trapped lithium. A Zeeman slower fed a dual magneto-optical trap; optical pumping prepared atoms for a cloverleaf apparatus for magnetic trapping of neutral atoms. Microwave evaporation removed energetic lithium-7 bosons; elastic collisions cooled lithium-6 fermions by sympathetic cooling.[ref]
Sequential absorption imaging recorded both trapped clouds on a camera. Fits to axial profiles used the boson cloud as a thermometer. At common temperature, the nearly equal magnetic trapping potentials provided a comparison: the clouds had similar sizes near T/TF​=1, but the fermion cloud remained broader as cooling reached T/TF​=0.25. Figure 3 compared its radius with ideal Fermi gas and classical predictions.[ref]
Varying the wait before imaging tested thermal equilibrium. Finite imaging resolution restricted the analysis to the axial direction; fits neglected interaction-induced density shifts. Cooling eventually suffered from the dwindling boson heat capacity. The result supports quantum occupation effects, without directly resolving individual occupied states or reaching zero temperature.[ref]
These were neutral alkali atoms in a spatially varying trap. The Fermi energy of a model electron gas instead uses uniform electrons, two equally populated spin states, and the electron mass. The measured trapped-atom radii are not measurements of that electron model's pF​ or EF​; comparing their numerical Fermi energies requires the appropriate particle mass, internal-state populations, and confining potential.

The quantum harmonic oscillator levels then have ϵ=ℏ(ωx​nx​+ωy​ny​+ωz​nz​) with nonnegative integer ni​ and reduced Planck constant ℏ=h/(2π).
When ϵ≫ℏωi​, counting lattice points can be approximated by the volume of a tetrahedron in the positive octant of (nx​,ny​,nz​):

This is a density of states, with units of inverse energy. The factor 1/6 is the unit tetrahedron volume; differentiating produces the factor 1/2. Treat the single ground state separately: its macroscopic population would be lost by replacing every level with a smooth density of states.

That finite excited-state capacity is the mechanism of Bose-Einstein condensation.
Set Nexsat​(Tc​)=N. Particle conservation gives, to this continuum accuracy,

Peierls transition

A Peierls transition, named for Rudolf Peierls, is a metal-insulator transition caused by a Peierls distortion of an initially metallic chain.[ref] A modulation at 2kF​ mixes states near opposite Fermi points and can open a band gap at the Fermi energy. At half filling with one atomic orbital per chemical atom, this modulation doubles the original lattice period and alternates strong and weak bonds. In a weak-coupling zero-temperature description, the Peierls energy gain is proportional to −(δ2/t)ln(t/∣δ∣) whereas the elastic cost is proportional to δ2, where t>0 is the undistorted hopping strength and δ its small alternating change. The logarithm permits a distortion at arbitrarily weak coupling in the ideal model. Finite temperature, finite size, interchain coupling and thermal fluctuations matter for a real transition; strictly one-dimensional reasoning alone does not establish finite-temperature long-range order.

A Peierls distortion modulates the atomic positions and chemical bonds of a one-dimensional chain with a partly filled energy band. In the half-filled example, alternating short and long bonds double the primitive unit cell. The distortion is the structural change; the associated Peierls transition is the change in electronic conduction.[ref]
Dimerized tight-binding chain (E±​(k)=±2t2cos2(ka)+δ2sin2(ka)​)
Words: 221 Articles: 1
Peierls distortion OurBigBook.com
For spin-degenerate electrons at atomic spacing a, alternate the hopping amplitudes −(t+δ) and −(t−δ), with t>0 and ∣δ∣<t. The doubled primitive unit cell gives an off-diagonal Bloch Hamiltonian entry −(t+δ)−(t−δ)e−2ika. Its two eigenvalues are the displayed energy bands, for ∣k∣≤π/(2a). The band gap at the edge of the Brillouin zone is 4∣δ∣. At half filling there are two electrons per doubled primitive unit cell, so the lower band is full and the upper empty. This explicit model realizes the period-doubling form of a Peierls distortion.
Logarithmic energy gain from a Peierls distortion (ΔE=−πt4δ2​log∣δ∣t​+O(δ2/t))
Words: 146
Dimerized tight-binding chain OurBigBook.com
Fill the lower energy band of the dimerized tight-binding chain with both spin states. Take zero on-site energy and measure ground-state energy per doubled primitive unit cell. State counting in a Bloch band and q=ka give
E(δ)=−π8​∫0π/2​t2cos2q+δ2sin2q​dq,E(0)=−π8t​.
(44)
Equivalently, for ∣δ∣≤t, E(δ)=−(8t/π)E(1−δ2/t2​), where E(k) is the complete elliptic integral of the second kind in the modulus convention.
For fixed t>0 and ∣δ∣/t→0, the change is
E(δ)−E(0)=−πt4δ2​log∣δ∣t​+O(δ2/t).​
(45)
The logarithm comes from states near the edge of the Brillouin zone. Put u=π/2−q. To leading order the square root there is t2u2+δ2​. For a fixed small cutoff η>0, direct integration gives
∫0η​[t2u2+δ2​−tu]du=2tδ2​log∣δ∣t​+O(δ2/t).
(46)
The rest of the band, and the higher-order corrections near its edge, contribute only O(δ2/t); multiplying by −8/π gives the displayed asymptotic expansion. Here the remainder uses Big O notation. The negative logarithmic term exceeds any fixed quadratic elastic cost Kδ2, K>0, for sufficiently small nonzero δ. This explains the zero-temperature instability to a Peierls distortion in the ideal chain model.
Electron-phonon scattering
Words: 339 Articles: 3
Electron-phonon interaction OurBigBook.com
In electron-phonon scattering, an electron changes its energy by ±ℏωq​ while its crystal momentum changes by a phonon wavevector modulo a reciprocal lattice vector. Charge-transport relaxation weights a scattering angle θ by 1−cosθ. Small-angle events can therefore relax heat efficiently while relaxing electrical current weakly. At temperatures above the phonon excitation scale, scattering becomes approximately elastic in the electron thermal shell; residual elastic disorder often dominates at very low temperature.
Electron-acoustic recoil length (λ=ℏ/(2me​cs​))
Words: 73
Electron-phonon scattering OurBigBook.com
For free-electron recoil and a linear acoustic branch, Ee​(q)=ℏ2q2/(2me​) and Eph​(q)=ℏcs​q. Their ratio is qλ, so equality occurs at q=1/λ. This is a momentum/localization crossover scale, formally half a sound-speed analogue of the Reduced Compton wavelength. It does not replace the speed of light in electron relativity or determine a mean free path. A Fermi-surface electron emitting a phonon has fractional radial loss δ≃q/(2λkF2​) when the transferred energy is small.
Electron-phonon Umklapp threshold
Words: 102
Electron-phonon scattering OurBigBook.com
For a spherical Fermi surface of radius kF​ lying inside a zone with shortest reciprocal lattice vector magnitude G>2kF​, a translated neighbouring Fermi sphere is separated from it by qU​=G−2kF​. An electron-phonon Umklapp scattering process satisfying k+q=k′+G therefore needs a phonon wavevector of at least qU​. For an approximately linear acoustic dispersion its activation scale is
TU​∼kB​ℏvs​(G−2kF​)​.
(47)
At T≪TU​ these phonons are sparsely occupied; once they become thermally available, momentum-relaxing scattering can grow rapidly. Normal small-angle scattering and residual disorder need not vanish below this scale, so it is a crossover estimate rather than a sharp universal conductivity threshold.
Small-angle electron-phonon transport at low temperature
Words: 98
Electron-phonon scattering OurBigBook.com
For acoustic modes ωq​≃cs​q, thermally active wavevectors have qT​∼kB​T/(ℏcs​). When qT​≪kF​, a nearly elastic event on a spherical Fermi surface has 1−cosθ=q2/(2kF2​), suppressing momentum relaxation. In the clean three-dimensional acoustic model, the thermal relaxation rate scales as T3 while the electrical transport rate gains two extra powers and scales as T5. With electronic heat capacity proportional to T, this gives Ke​∝T−2 and electrical resistivity proportional to T5 in the phonon-limited regime. Residual elastic scattering cuts off these behaviours as temperature falls further.[ref]
Phonon scattering
Words: 239 Articles: 3
Phonon OurBigBook.com
Phonon scattering changes the occupation or propagation of lattice-vibration normal modes through interactions with boundaries, defects or other phonons. Anharmonic terms permit phonon-phonon scattering. Different processes need not relax heat flow equally: normal processes conserve total crystal momentum within the first Brillouin zone, whereas Umklapp scattering changes its representative by a nonzero reciprocal lattice vector.
Normal phonon collisions and heat-current relaxation
Words: 65
Phonon scattering OurBigBook.com
Normal phonon collisions conserve the crystal momentum of the distribution, whereas Umklapp scattering transfers momentum by a reciprocal vector. A normal collision can redistribute heat-carrying modes without relaxing a drifting distribution in the same manner as a momentum-relaxing event. Boundaries, impurities and Umklapp processes can then set the resistance. Counting all collision rates as interchangeable inverse transport times can miss collective phonon flow and nontrivial current weighting.
Phonon mean free path (ℓ=vg​τ)
Words: 54
Phonon scattering OurBigBook.com
The phonon mean free path is the typical distance traveled by a phonon between the relevant scattering events. For heat transport, the relevant relaxation time must describe relaxation of heat current, not merely count all collisions. An isotropic kinetic estimate is κ≃cV​vs​ℓ/3, where cV​ is heat capacity per unit volume. Boundary-limited ℓ and the low-temperature Debye model give κ∝T3.
Umklapp scattering (q1​+q2​−q3​=G=0)
Words: 76
Phonon scattering OurBigBook.com
An Umklapp process conserves reduced crystal momentum modulo a nonzero reciprocal lattice vector. It can occur in electron-phonon scattering as well as phonon-phonon scattering; the lattice takes up the reciprocal-lattice momentum.
In a three-phonon Umklapp scattering process, the first-zone wavevectors obey the displayed equation for a nonzero reciprocal lattice vector G, together with conservation of energy. The crystal momentum transferred to the lattice allows these processes to relax a phonon heat current. They are suppressed at sufficiently low temperature and often determine the approximate 1/T high-temperature thermal conductivity of a crystalline electrical insulator.
Debye–Waller factor
Words: 59
Phonon OurBigBook.com
The Debye–Waller factor suppresses coherent scattering because atoms fluctuate about their equilibrium positions. For Gaussian displacement u, the amplitude factor is ⟨eiqu⟩=exp[−q2⟨u2⟩/2] and the intensity factor is its squared modulus. It multiplies the lattice interference factor, so exact extrema of the full finite-lattice intensity need not coincide with the constructive-interference centers when this envelope varies appreciably.

Phonon OurBigBook.com
For a chain with lattice spacing b and N atoms, write xs​=sb+us​. The periodic normal-mode condition is uN​=u0​, equivalently xN​=x0​+Nb for unwrapped positions. The literal position condition xN​=x0​ is incompatible with the equilibrium xs​=sb in that coordinate system. Fourier modes kr​=2πr/(Nb) give ωr​=2λ∣sin(kr​b/2)∣ for spring coefficient mλ2. The zero mode describes free center-of-mass translation and must be fixed or handled separately when defining an oscillator vacuum.

Long-range harmonic-chain dispersion OurBigBook.com
Let α=C2​/C1​>0 and x=sin2(ka/2). The squared frequency in units 4C1​/M is (1+4α)x−4αx2. For α≤1/4 its maximum on 0≤x≤1 is at the zone edge and equals one. For α>1/4 it moves inside the zone to x=(1+4α)/(8α), with the displayed frequency ratio. The small-wavevector speed instead increases by 1+4α​; maximizing the frequency and finding the sound speed are different operations.

Words: 34
Phonon dispersion relation OurBigBook.com
A continuous family of normal modes labelled by the wavevector and a branch index s. For r chemical atoms per three-dimensional primitive unit cell, the dynamical matrix has 3r eigenvalues, giving 3r branches: three acoustic phonon branches and 3r−3 optical phonon branches for a mechanically stable ordinary crystal structure.
Extended-zone representation of a phonon dispersion
Words: 51
Phonon dispersion relation OurBigBook.com
The crystal momentum of a phonon is defined modulo a reciprocal lattice vector. Extending its dispersion relation periodically beyond the first Brillouin zone labels equivalent excitations by different extended wavevectors. A scattering transfer Q=G+q can be outside that zone while its reduced phonon wavevector q is inside. The measured neutron recoil depends on the actual transfer Q, not on the reduced representative alone.

Diatomic-chain zone-edge polarizations (ωac2​=2α/M,ωop2​=2α/m)
Words: 72
Diatomic-chain dispersion relation with equal springs OurBigBook.com
In an alternating-mass chain with nearest-neighbour spacing a and cell length 2a, the inter-sublattice Bloch coupling is proportional to cosqa. At the first-zone edge q=π/(2a) it vanishes. For M>m, the acoustic edge mode moves only the heavy sublattice and the optical edge mode only the light one. Their frequency difference is 2α/m​−2α/M​. At long wavelength the acoustic displacements are in phase, whereas the optical mode has zero centre-of-mass displacement.

Diatomic-chain dispersion relation with equal springs OurBigBook.com
For alternating masses mA​,mB​, nearest-neighbour spacing a and equal spring constants α, the zone-centre optical angular frequency and acoustic group velocity obey
ωop2​(0)=2α(mA​1​+mB​1​),vs2​=mA​+mB​2αa2​.

Therefore α=mA​mB​ωop2​(0)/[2(mA​+mB​)] and a=vs​(mA​+mB​)/(2α)​. These infer effective model parameters from a measured intercept and initial slope of a phonon dispersion relation. Fitting a real polar crystal to a nearest-neighbour scalar model does not guarantee that every measured point or its structural spacing is reproduced exactly.

The Debye model replaces the crystal's vibrational spectrum by a continuum of phonon modes up to a cutoff chosen to preserve the total number of vibrational degrees of freedom.

For T≪ΘD​, expand (ex−1)−1=∑j≥1​e−jx and integrate termwise: the limiting integral is 2∑j≥1​j−3=2ζ(3). This counts thermal quanta, not available modes or half quanta of zero-point energy.

Mode count in the Debye model (β=512π4​ΘD3​Nm​kB​​,kD3​=6π2Nm​/V)
Words: 156
Debye model OurBigBook.com
Suppose a three-dimensional Debye model is normalized to 3Nm​ vibrational modes in volume V. Its low-temperature heat-capacity coefficient is the one displayed, and its spherical wavevector cutoff obeys kD3​=6π2Nm​/V. The Debye temperature is ΘD​=ℏvD​kD​/kB​. At fixed measured β and volume, changing the counting convention by Nm​↦cNm​ raises both ΘD​ and kD​ by c1/3; the inferred average sound speed is unchanged.
For a mole of formula units containing r atoms each, a conventional full atomic-mode count uses Nm​=rNA​ and tends to lattice heat capacity 3rR at high temperature. A reduced convention using Nm​=NA​ instead has three effective modes per formula unit. These are different continuum normalizations, not a claim that the real crystal has only three modes per formula unit. A real multi-atom primitive cell has three acoustic branches and additional optical branches; a Debye sphere preserving the full atomic count is an effective representation of that spectrum, rather than its literal first Brillouin zone.

If a stipulated electron-phonon scattering model makes resistivity proportional to this phonon number with a temperature-independent coefficient, the high-temperature electrical resistivity is proportional to T.

Differentiate at fixed volume and substitute x=ℏω/(kB​T) to obtain the displayed heat capacity at constant volume.
At T≪ΘD​, integration by parts gives ∫0∞​x4ex/(ex−1)2dx=4∫0∞​x3/(ex−1)dx=4π4/15. Therefore CV​∼(12π4/5)NkB​(T/ΘD​)3.
